chunks: Then, beware of destroying your manners and changing them,

and make the tongue one, and let a man guard his tongue, for this tongue is obstinate with its master. By Allah, I do not see a servant who fears Allah with a fear that benefits him unless he guards his tongue,
and certainly the tongue of the believer is behind his heart, and the heart of the hypocrite is behind his tongue;
because when the believer intends to speak a word, he reflects upon it in himself. If it is good, he reveals it, and if it is bad, he conceals it,
and the hypocrite speaks whatever comes to his tongue, not knowing what is for him and what is against him.

key_terms.تَدَبَّرَهُ: he reflected upon it or pondered it
key_terms.جَمُوحٌ: obstinate, unruly, or hard to control

ai.seo_question: How does the behavior of a believer's tongue differ from that of a hypocrite according to Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: Imam Ali (AS) highlights the tongue as a restless force that must be disciplined by the heart, a core tenet of Shia ethical scholarship where inner sincerity (ikhlas) dictates outward speech. This narration underscores the psychological distinction between the believer, who exercises deliberate restraint (hilm), and the hypocrite, whose speech reveals a disconnect between heart and tongue, a concept frequently analyzed in Tafsir al-Mi'qdad.
